why: the claim took its rounds and did not close
claim: Type `01 60`'s pitch bytes are not read by anything that runs at a rate of its own. They are read out of a window, and the output repeats every time the read-out has drifted that window's length -- so the rate a take carries is `|r - 1| / T`, where `r` is the ratio the two pitch bytes ask for and `T` is the window. Across the coarse byte the ratio was moved from a quarter to double, which is `|r - 1|` from 0.056 to 1.000, and the rate moved with it from 0.90 to 15.63 Hz: over that factor of eighteen `T` stays between 62.1 and 64.7 ms. At unison the line is not slow, it is gone -- byte 64 returns 4.81 Hz, which is this voice's own amplitude wobble and the same figure the fine byte returns at its own unison. On the fine byte, which reaches ratios three orders closer to one than the coarse byte's smallest step does, the four settings whose implied rate clears the run's own floor of 0.3033 Hz come back at 0.4504 to 0.9384 Hz and give `T` of 63.21 to 63.74 ms, while every setting between them returns the voice's wobble instead -- which is what a window rate under the floor looks like and is not something a clock of the stage's own could do. The byte the page prints `Shift Mode` against, over five states and with no unit beside them, moves `T` and moves nothing else. Its five states return 32.00, 42.68, 63.78, 85.27 and 128.0 ms, which is the ratio 3 : 4 : 6 : 8 : 12, read at two shifts an octave apart. The shortest is 1024 steps of the 32000 Hz clock this archive already reads this unit's delay ladder as cut to; the third is 2048 of them and the fifth is 4096, so three of the five are successive powers of two and the two between them sit a fourth and a fifth along -- two octaves reached in four steps. Read at the octave, where the two shortest windows put the rate past the 20 Hz ceiling this reading searches to, those two and only those two come back at exactly half: 15.6261 where 31.25 is asked for, and 11.7221 where 23.44 is.
named: a time-domain splicer: one window read out at the pitch ratio and re-entered every time the read-out has drifted the window's length, with a mode byte that picks which of five windows is used
adds: Nothing structural had been read on this type. The archive held no reading of either pitch byte and none of the mode byte, whose page prints five numbered states and no unit at all -- so what the number counted was not merely unknown, it had no candidate quantity. This says what it is the length of, and it says it in the unit the rest of this machine's delays are already measured in. It also supplies the one thing a pitch byte's own sweep cannot: a null. A shifter asked for no shift produces no splice, so the setting at the middle of both bytes is the run's own control and it sits inside the sweep rather than beside it.
refutedBy: Any setting whose measured rate is not `|r - 1|` over a window the mode byte alone decides. Two shapes of that: a coarse sweep returning one rate rather than one length, which is what a clock of the stage's own would give and is what the eighteenfold sweep was made to look for; or a mode byte that moves the rate at a fixed shift by anything other than the ratio it moves it by at a different shift, which is what a mode byte selecting something other than a length would give. Separately, a rate at unison. The claim says the splice stops there, so a line at byte 64 that is not the line the bypassed voice carries refutes it outright.
whatItWouldChange: Rendering this type needs a window and a read-out ratio, not an interpolator with a rate. Which window is the mode byte's whole job, and the five it selects are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 6 : 8 : 12.

A page that prints five numbered states with no unit beside them has been read here as a length. Any other slot on this machine printing a bare count where a quantity is expected may be one too, and the measurement that settles it is a sweep of something else while the counted byte is held.
The artefact rate of this type is predictable from the two pitch bytes and the mode byte alone, so a file asking for a shift can be told what it will hear without the unit being asked.

alternatives.reading: A clock inside the stage runs at a fixed rate and the pitch bytes only change what is read out, so the periodicity is the clock's and not a drift's.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: A fixed clock returns one rate down a sweep. The coarse byte moves the rate from 0.8800 to 15.6290 Hz, a factor of 17.8, and does it monotonically in `|r - 1|` on both sides of unison -- 0.9353 at a ratio above one and 0.8800 at the one an equal distance below. What stays fixed across that is the length the two imply, not the rate.

alternatives.reading: The periodicity is the shifted voice beating against the direct path, which is what any two copies a semitone apart do.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: A beat between two copies of a tone is at `|r - 1|` times the tone's own frequency, so on this carrier the major third would beat at 114 Hz and the octave at 440. The readings are 4.08 and 15.63 Hz. The run also put the balance at the top of its byte and the second shifter's level at nought, so the direct path is out of the mixture and there is no second copy to beat with.

alternatives.reading: The shift is done in the frequency domain, and the periodicity is the transform's own hop rather than a splice.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: A hop is a property of the transform and not of the shift, so it would return one rate at every ratio -- the same reading the fixed clock alternative is refuted by. It would also not vanish at unison, where a transform still hops and this stage returns the bypassed voice's own line.

alternatives.reading: `T` is the interval between splices and the window read out is longer than it, overlapped and crossfaded, so the length named here is not the length of anything stored.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The output was read for a copy of itself, off takes already recorded, by the stage this archive reads its delay ladder with. It holds one, at half the window the mode byte selects, at four of the five states and on both shifters, landing within a twentieth of a per cent while the windows themselves are a third apart. A read-out spliced at its own length holds one copy at a time and leaves no such peak. So the read-out is overlapped, as this alternative said, and the length named by the claim is the length of something stored, which is what this alternative denied. What is left of it -- whether the pair is stored a window apart or half a window apart, which one shift cannot separate -- is recorded as what the round did not settle rather than left standing here.

alternatives.reading: The two shifters have a window each, and what was measured is the first one's rather than a property of the type.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The mirror run was made: the same five states of the mode byte with `L.Bal` at the top of its byte, the second shifter's own coarse byte carrying the octave and the first one's at unison. The five lengths come back the same. The worst the two shifters disagree by is under five parts in ten thousand, against five windows whose closest neighbours are a third apart, and it is the size of what one shifter's repeat of a single state already costs. What is not separated by it -- one shared buffer against two configured alike -- is a different reading and is recorded as equivalent under this test rather than left standing as this one.

extra.key: why the unison row is the control
extra.text: The run's null is a setting of the sweep rather than a take beside it. A shifter asked for no shift has nothing to splice, so the middle of both pitch bytes is a state that certainly carries no rate of the effect's -- and it is the one setting where the reading has to come back with the voice. It does: 4.8052 Hz on the coarse sweep and 4.8107 on the fine, both on all four partials, against 4.79 to 4.82 Hz read off this archive's own bypassed takes of the same held tone. That is what makes the lines at every other setting attributable to the byte rather than to the note.

extra.key: a reading that moved after this was made
extra.text: One figure moved on a republication this claim did not ask for, and it moved towards what the claim predicts. The coarse byte one semitone below unison was published at 0.9040 hertz and is now 0.8800. The rate read here is the ratio's distance from one over the window, and at this setting that is 0.0561 over 63.78 milliseconds, which is 0.880. The old figure was the reading resolving a tie between two of its partials by the order they arrived in; the new one is the pair that agreed. Nothing was fitted to make it move, and the setting was not one this claim's window was measured from.

extra.key: a row that declined after this was made
extra.text: The mode byte's longest state at a major third stopped naming a rate under the same change and now publishes the pair its partials split between. This claim already rested on that row twice over: it cites the row's own per-partial rates beside the rate, and it was the weakest of the five there -- which is why the whole sweep was taken again an octave up, where every state returns four times the rate and this one repeats. The octave pass is what the five lengths stand on, and it did not move.

extra.key: what the unison row also carries
extra.text: The control above is a control of the rate reading and of nothing else, and this says what the same takes turned out to hold when a different reading was put on them. A shifter asked for no shift splices nothing, so the row carries no rate of the effect's and the rate reading came back with the voice, which is what made the lines elsewhere attributable to the byte. It does carry a distance: read for a copy of the output in itself, the same two takes hold one a whole window apart. The two are not in conflict -- a rate is how often something repeats and a distance is how far apart two copies sit, and a pair that neither drifts nor splices has the second and not the first -- but the sentence above was written before anything had read these takes that way, and a state that carries no rate is not a state that carries nothing.
